summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal in Guinea-Bissau. Decree 4/93, the 1993 penal code, omits same-sex offences, and the country has never criminalised them. The U.S. Department of State's 2011 and 2012 human rights reports both record no criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct.

Guinea-Bissau has no trans framework of any kind. No legal gender recognition procedure exists, no partnership or marriage recognition exists for same-sex couples, and no anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, education, health care or public life. The U.S. Department of State's 2012 report found that antidiscrimination laws do not apply to LGBT individuals, and found no official discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in access to health care, employment or education.

Article 5, the principle of equality, of the Law on Prevention, Protection and Combating Domestic Violence (Law No. 6/2014) states that all victims, regardless of sexual orientation, enjoy the fundamental rights inherent to human dignity and are guaranteed equal opportunities to a life free from violence as well as physical and mental health. The provision addresses sexual orientation and does not name gender identity.

Guinea-Bissau signed the 2008 UN statement on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The state recognises no same-sex partnerships. Only married heterosexual couples are entitled to family-size government housing under civil-service housing allowance guidelines; same-sex couples receive the single-person allotment. The U.S. Department of State recorded this rule in both its 2011 and its 2012 reports.

The dominant visitor risk is the weakness of the protection machinery rather than a specific statute. The U.S. Department of State's 2012 report on Guinea-Bissau documents the 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and impunity. Its 2011 report documents torture by security forces, female genital mutilation and the same culture of impunity. The same 2012 report found no reported violent incidents or human rights abuses targeting people on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, but in 2018 a local NGO director stated that there were some cases of violence targeting people on that basis and that Guinea-Bissau lacks legal protections for LGBTI people.

Social attitudes are mixed. The 2011 report noted societal stigma against LGBT people, and the 2012 report found that social taboos sometimes restricted freedom to express sexual orientation, while describing society as relatively tolerant of consensual same-sex conduct. A 2010 Pew Research Center survey of 19 African countries placed Guinea-Bissau among the most tolerant: nine percent said homosexual behaviour was morally acceptable and fifteen percent said it was not an issue. There is no visible LGBT scene.
tangentialFactors:
The 2012 coup and the documented pattern of arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and impunity shape what any visitor can expect from the authorities, including in complaints about violence. Weak rule of capacity means a legal right on paper may yield little practical remedy.

The government housing rule is a concrete form of state-level differential treatment: only married heterosexual couples qualify for family-size government housing, while same-sex couples receive the single-person allotment. The rule was documented independently in the 2011 and 2012 U.S. Department of State reports.

Regional comparison matters for expectation-setting. Guinea-Bissau's nine percent moral-acceptability figure placed it among the more tolerant of 19 African countries surveyed in 2010, a profile a traveller would not necessarily expect for the region. One country guide scores travel safety at 34 out of 100, a caution rating.

Female genital mutilation is documented by the U.S. Department of State as widespread, relevant to health and protection concerns for women and girls travelling or resident.
localsOnly:
Residents have no avenue to obtain legal gender recognition, and there is no statutory route for amending gender markers on identity documents.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or register a partnership, and adoption rules do not address LGBTQ applicants. A French government website states that single and married people are eligible to adopt, without indicating whether LGBTQ people are disqualified.

Article 5 of Law No. 6/2014 gives victims of domestic violence, regardless of sexual orientation, guaranteed rights to a life free from violence and to physical and mental health. Enforcement of that guarantee is not documented in the sourced record.

Civil-service housing allowance guidelines restrict family-size government housing to heterosexual married couples, which reduces the household benefit available to same-sex couples and to single staff.

There is no anti-discrimination law available to LGBT residents in employment, education, health care or services, and hate-crime provisions addressing sexual orientation or gender identity are absent from the sourced material.
outOfScopeNotes:
Nothing in the sourced record documents a document-amendment procedure or a border-screening pathway for trans travellers arriving in Guinea-Bissau, and none can be assumed. Whether immigration officers inspect gender markers, and what follows from a mismatch, is unresolved.

The sources do not address gender-marker rules on passports used for entry, nor whether consular or airline screening creates an outing risk.

The 2018 reports of violence targeting people on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity are asserted without dates, locations, perpetrators or outcomes. The scale and pattern of such violence remain unresolved.

Adoption eligibility for LGBTQ applicants is unresolved: one government website describes who may adopt without stating whether LGBTQ people are excluded.

No youth-specific or minor-specific health access findings, and no findings specific to trans or LGBTQ minors, school students or youth travellers, appear in the sources. There are also no sourced findings on facility access, on restrictions or requirements affecting trans people's medical care, or on penalties for hate-motivated violence.
